                                                 Noise sensitivity of crossings for high temperature Ising
                                                                           model
                                                                      Vincent Tassion∗ Hugo Vanneuville†




arXiv:2505.11457v2 [math.PR] 6 Aug 2025
                                                                                       Abstract
                                                      Consider the event that there is a + crossing from left to right in a box for the
                                                  Ising model on the triangular lattice. We show that this event is noise sensitive
                                                  under Glauber dynamics t 7→ σt in the subcritical regime β < βc . We rely on
                                                  the non-spectral approach from our previous work [TV23]. An important aspect
                                                  in this more general setup is the study of the pair (σ0 , σt ) and in particular the
                                                  establishment of properties such as finite-energy and spatial mixing.

1     Introduction
1.1    Noise sensitivity
The concept of noise sensitivity was introduced by Benjamini, Kalai and Schramm
in [BKS99] for critical planar Bernoulli percolation. In this model, each site of the
triangular lattice is first colored black or white independently with probability 1/2.
Then, the resulting configuration evolves in time by resampling each site at rate 1.
They considered the event that a large rectangle is crossed from left to right and
proved that this event is noise sensitive: for every fixed t > 0 (even very small), its
occurrence at time 0 and time t are asymptotically independent. A refinement of the
result was later obtained by Schramm and Steif [SS10] using randomized algorithms.
Then, Garban, Pete and Schramm [GPS10] obtained a precise description of the
phenomenon by identifying the amount of noise implying asymptotic independence.
    Noise sensitivity has also been proven for other planar critical percolation mod-
els: Bernoulli percolation under exclusion dynamics [BGS13, GV19], dynamical
Bernoulli percolation in a Liouville environment [GHSS21], Poisson Boolean per-
colation [ABGM14], Voronoi percolation [AGMT16, AB18, Van21] and percolation
of nodal lines [GV20]. We refer to the book [GS14] for more about noise sensitiv-
ity and its motivations. All of these results rely on a study of the dynamics via
Fourier methods. In [TV23], we gave a new proof of the sharp noise sensitivity
theorem of [GPS10] by relying on differential inequalities, inspired by the work of
Kesten [Kes87] on near-critical percolation. One motivation was to provide a more
robust approach than the Fourier method. In the present paper, we apply it to high
temperature Ising model evolving under Glauber dynamics.

1.2    Noise sensitivity for high temperature Ising model
Consider the regular planar triangular lattice and let T denote the set of sites of this
lattice, that is, T = {n + meiπ/3 : n, m ∈ Z}. If x, y ∈ T, we write x ∼ y to say that
{x, y} is an edge of the triangular lattice, i.e. |x − y| = 1, where | · | is the Euclidean
norm. Let n ≥ 1 and x ∈ T. We consider the rhombus

                     Λn = k + meiπ/3 ∈ T : k, m ∈ {−n, . . . , n} .
                           

If x ∈ T, we let Λn (x) = x + Λn be the rhombus centered at x. When we say
rhombus in this paper, we always refer to a set of this type. Given a rhombus Λ and


                                            2
some δ > 0, we let Λ(δ) denote the ‘thickened rhombus’ whose center is the same
as Λ and whose sides have been scaled by factor 1 + δ (with the convention that
here and in all the paper we consider the ceil of the new size of sides to work with
integer-valued sides).
   Let
                                  Ωn = {−1, +1}Λn
denote the set of all spin configurations in Λn .
Definition 1.1 (Ising measure with free boundary conditions). Let n ≥ 1 and let
E(Λn ) denote the set of edges whose endpoints are both in Λn . The energy of a spin
configuration η ∈ Ωn is
                                        X
                           H(η) = −             η(x)η(y).
                                      {x,y}∈E(Λn )

Given some β ∈ (0, +∞), the Ising measure at inverse temperature β (with free
boundary conditions and no external field) on Λn is the probability measure µn =
µn,β on Ωn defined by
                                         1             
                       ∀η ∈ Ωn    µn (η) = exp − βH(η) ,
                                        Zn
                                             P
where Zn = Zn,β is the renormalizing constant η∈Ωn exp(−βH(η)).
    In this paper, we prove noise sensitivity properties of crossing events, that we
define now.
Definition 1.2. For every n ≥ 1, we let Crossn ⊂ Ω2n denote the event that there
is a path included in Λn from the left side of this rhombus to its right side, that is
only made of +1 spins. We study the crossing of Λn for spin configurations in the
larger rhombus Λ2n to avoid boundary effects.
   Let β ∈ (0, +∞), n ≥ 1 and let σ ∼ µ2n = µ2n,β . By symmetry of the rhombus
and of the measure µ2n and by self-duality, we have
                                                  1
                         P σ ∈ Crossn = µ2n Crossn = .
                                                    2
We consider a dynamics (σs )s≥0 defined by sampling σ0 = σ ∼ µn and letting
it evolve according to Glauber resampling dynamics: we associate Poisson clocks
to every site and, every time a clock rings, the value of the corresponding spin is
resampled (under the law of this spin conditionally on the value of the neighbouring
spins). This dynamics is defined more precisely in Section 1.5. The main result
of our paper is that the crossing events in the Ising model at inverse temperature
β < βc are sensitive under Glauber dynamics (see the appendix for the definition
of βc ).
Theorem 1.3 (Noise sensitivity). Let β < βc . For any t > 0,
                                        
                        P σ, σt ∈ Crossn −→ 1/4,
                                                 n→+∞

where (σs )s≥0 is the Glauber dynamics in Λ2n (with free boundary conditions), at
inverse temperature β and starting from σ ∼ µ2n (as defined in Section 1.5).


                                             3
      Remarks:
          • We stress that even if the model is subcritical from the point of view of
            spin/spin correlations (i.e. β < βc ), it is critical from the point of view of
            percolation observables (for instance, crossing probabilities are bounded away
            from 0 and 1, see Section 2.1.2).
          • Readers are probably wondering about the cases β = βc and β > βc . In both
            these cases, the crossing events are not noise sensitive anymore.1 The reason
            is that the exponent of the four-arm event (see Definition 1.4) is larger than 2
            in these cases. More precisely, if we use the notations from Section 1.3, then
            αn ≤ n−(2+c) for some c > 0 if β = βc (see the work of Wu [Wu18]) and αn
            even decays exponentially fast if β > βc . The general differential formulas (see
            e.g. Section 2.2.2) that we use in this paper then imply that, for every t > 0,
            P(σ, σt ∈ Crossn ) → 1/2.
          • We stated the result for the crossing event of a rhombus, but the proof adapts
            directly to more general shapes, for instance with Λn replaced by a ρn × n
            rectangle for some fixed ρ > 0.
          • We have chosen to work in finite volume in the whole paper. Another possibil-
            ity could have been to sample σ according to the Gibbs measure µ at inverse
            temperature β in infinite volume (which is unique when β < βc )2 and let this
            configuration evolve according to the Glauber dynamics in infinite volume. We
            have preferred to work only in finite volume in order to be able to ignore sev-
            eral technical issues (in particular in the derivation of differential formulas).
            The (essentially unique) drawback is that translation invariance does not hold
            but is replaced by a ‘quasi-invariance by translation’, see Section 5.3.
      Concerning other questions related to noise sensitivity in the Ising model, see in
      particular the work of Galicza and Pete [GP24] (who prove that no sparse recon-
      struction is possible for transitive functions in the regime β < βc ) and the work
      of Broman and Steif [BS05] (about stability properties in Ising models that are
      non-critical from the point of view of percolation observables).

      1.3     Sharp noise sensitivity
      Our analysis is actually quantitative and we obtain the sharp noise sensitivity the-
      orem, i.e. the analogue of the theorem obtained by Garban, Pete and Schramm
      [GPS10] for Bernoulli percolation evolving under i.i.d. dynamics. To state this the-
      orem, we need to define the 4-arm event.
      Definition 1.4. Let β ∈ (0, +∞) and n ≥ 1. We let A4 (n) ⊂ Ω2n denote the event
      that there are four paths from a neighbour of the origin o := (0, 0) to ∂Λn := {x ∈
      Λn : ∃y ∈ T \ Λn : y ∼ x}, such that each path is of constant sign and the signs of
      the four paths alternate around o. A4 (n) is called the ‘4-arm event’. We let
                              αn = µ2n (A4 (n))   and εn = 1/(n2 αn ).
      Remark 1.5. It can help to keep in mind that, if β < βc , then there exist c, C > 0
      such that εn ≤ Cn−c for every n ≥ 1 (see Section 2.1.2).
   1
     At least they are not noise sensitive at a fixed time t > 0. The question of rather studying the
sensitivity at a time that equals a constant times the relaxation time might be a more natural question.
   2
     See e.g. [FV17] for the definition of this measure.


                                                   4
         The noise sensitivity property Theorem 1.3 is a consequence of the following
      theorem (and of Remark 1.5).
      Theorem 1.6 (Sharp noise sensitivity). Let β < βc and let (tn )n≥1 be a sequence
      of non-negative numbers.
         • If tn /εn → +∞, then P σ, σtn ∈ Crossn → 1/4;
                                                  

         • If tn /εn → 0, then P σ, σtn ∈ Crossn → 1/2;
                                                

      where (σs )s≥0 is the Glauber dynamics in Λ2n (with free boundary conditions), at
      inverse temperature β and starting from σ ∼ µ2n (as defined in Section 1.5).
         The main novelty in the theorem above is the first item (noise region). Indeed,
      the second item (stability region) could be derived from the arguments in [GPS18,
      Section 8].

      1.4    Strategy of the proof
      To prove the noise sensitivity theorems, we follow the approach from our work
      [TV23], which in the present context consists in studying differential inequalities
      satisfied by t 7→ P(σ, σt ∈ A) for percolation-type events A. We prove that, when t
      is small enough, the pair (σ, σt ) essentially satisfies all the desired general properties
      to run this proof. In particular:
         • (Finite-energy). Changing the spin value at times 0 and t at some fixed vertex
           has a cost bounded independently of the rest of the configuration.
         • (Spatial mixing, when β ≤ βc ). The configuration in a box is quasi-independent
           of the configuration at macroscopic distance from it. A typical application is
           about arm events: let A1 (m, n) be the one-arm event, that is, the event that
           there is a path made of spins +1 from ∂Λm to ∂Λn . If n ≥ 2m then

                  P(σ, σt ∈ A1 (1, n)) ≤ C · P(σ, σt ∈ A1 (1, m))P(σ, σt ∈ A1 (2m, n)).

         • (Russo-type differential formula). The derivative of t 7→ P(σ, σt ∈ A) can be
           expressed in terms of pivotal events for the event A. This essentially follows
           from standard derivative formulas for Markovian dynamics, together with the
           above-mentioned finite-energy property.
      The first two properties are known for the static Ising model (i.e. for σ instead
      of (σ, σt )) and in this case essentially follow from the spatial Markov property of
      this model. Such a direct approach seems delicate since the pair (σ, σt ) does not
      satisfy the spatial Markov property.3 Instead, we decompose static and dynamical
      influences. More precisely the spin at some site x at time 0 can influence the spin
      at some other site y at time t through two mechanisms: Either the spin at x has
      already influenced the spin at y at time 0, which can be estimated by using the
      properties of the static Ising model. Or the information of the value of the spin at
      x has traveled through time, which we estimate using that the set of sites that have
      rung before time t is a subcritical percolation (provided t is small enough) and that
      the dynamics is local (the probability that a spin changes when a clock rings only
      depends on the neighbours of the site).
  3
    For more about this lack of spatial Markov property for the pair, see the sketch of proof from
Section 3.2.


                                                  5
    Finite-energy, spatial mixing and a Russo-type formula are proven in Sections 3, 4
and 5. Then, the percolation arguments inspired from [TV23] are done in Sections 6
and 7. Most of the work in these last sections consists of proving the so-called quasi-
multiplicativity property for the quantities P[a 4-arm event holds at times 0 and t].
The general strategy is standard, but new difficulties emerge due to possible inter-
actions between −1 paths at time 0 and +1 paths at time t. See Section 6 (and in
particular the paragraph below Proposition 6.5).

1.5    Setup
In this section, we introduce the general setup we will be working with in the rest
of the paper. More precisely, in Definition 1.8 below, we define a Glauber dynamics
in Λn . Each time we refer to the ‘Glauber dynamics in Λn ’ in this paper, we refer
to the dynamical process (σs )s≥0 that is introduced in this definition. Let us fix
some β ∈ (0, +∞) once and for all in this section and let us first introduce some
notations:
   • If n ≥ 1, η ∈ Ωn and x ∈ Λn , we let η x ∈ Ωn be the spin configuration obtained
     from η by just flipping the spin at x;
   • We define the ‘rates’ cx : Ωn → [0, 1] by

                                µn (η x )                1
                cx (η) =                  x
                                            =           P                .
                           µn (η) + µn (η )   1 + exp 2β y∈Λn :y∼x ηx ηy

      N.B: cx (η) only depends on the value of η at x and its neighbours and is equal
      to the probability that the spin at x equals −η(x) conditionally on the event
      that the spin configuration coincides with η at the neighbours of x.
Remark 1.7. The rates cx defined above correspond to the so-called Glauber heat-
bath dynamics. All of our analysis would also work in the case of the so-called
Glauber Metropolis dynamics, where cx (η) is replaced by min{1, µn (η x )/µn (η)}.
Definition 1.8 (Glauber dynamics). Given some n ≥ 1, we define a continuous time
dynamical process (σs )s≥0 on Ωn called ‘Glauber dynamics in Λn ’ (with free bound-
ary conditions and no external field). This process is defined on some probability
space (Ω, F, P) and is constructed as follows:
   • We sample σ ∼ µn and we let σ0 = σ;
   • We associate a Poisson Point Process Yx of parameter 1 on R+ (a ‘Poisson
     clock’) to every x ∈ Λn , independently for every x and independently of σ;
   • We let (Ux,i )x∈Λn ,i≥1 be a family of independent variables that are uniform in
     [0, 1] and are independent of σ and the Poisson clocks;
   • If the clock on a vertex x has rung for the ith time at some time t, then we
     flip the corresponding spin if Ux,i ≥ 1 − cx (σt− ).
We let Y = (Yx )x∈Λn and U = (Ux,i )x∈Λn ,i≥1 .
    We have thus defined a continuous time càdlàg Markov process with values in
Ωn . See for instance [Lig85, Chapter 4] more about this process. It is important to
bear in mind that this process starts from its invariant measure µn , and that this
measure is reversible.




                                           6
Some conventions about vocabulary and notations. In all the paper,
given some n ≥ 1, the sentence ‘A is a static event’ means that A is a subset of Ωn
and, given some V ⊆ Λn , the sentence ‘A is a static event that depends only on V ’
means that A is a subset of Ωn such that 1A (η ′ ) = 1A (η) for every spin configurations
η, η ′ ∈ Ωn that coincide in V . In order to make the difference between static and
dynamical events, we use letters A, B, . . . to denote static events, i.e. subsets of Ωn ,
and letters A, B, . . . to denote dynamical events, i.e. elements of the σ-algebra F
from Definition 1.8. We use the letter η to denote a fixed spin configuration (i.e.
an element of Ωn ) and, as the reader can see in Definition 1.8, σ is a random spin
configuration sampled according to µn and (σs )s≥0 is the Ising Glauber dynamics
in Λn that starts from σ.

Boundaries. If V ⊆ T, we let ∂V = {x ∈ V : ∃y ∈ T \ V, y ∼ x} and ∂ext V =
{x ∈ T \ V : ∃y ∈ V, y ∼ x}.

Conventions about constants. In all the paper, the constants c, C, c′ , C ′ ,
c0 , C0 are positive finite constants that are independent of everything except the
inverse temperature β. Sometimes, the constants will depend on a parameter δ. In
this case, we will use the notations cδ , Cδ . In the proofs, we will often omit the
constants and rather use the notations ≲ and ≍: if f, g are positive functions, we
write f ≲ g if there exists C > 0 such that f ≤ Cg and we write f ≍ g if f ≲ g and
g ≲ f.

2     Background
2.1     Background on static Ising model
2.1.1    Three properties
Let us start this subsection with a preliminary remark: In the present section, we
consider the Ising model on some general finite set V ⊂ T and with some general
boundary conditions. We will consider the Ising model in this generality a few times
but we will mostly work with the Ising measure µn with free boundary conditions on
Λn , so the notations from this subsection will in fact only appear very occasionally.
    Let β ∈ (0, +∞), let us also fix some finite set V ⊂ T and recall that ∂ext V =
{x ∈ T \ V : ∃y ∈ V, y ∼ x}. Moreover, let ξ be a boundary condition on V , that
is, an element of {−1, 0, +1}∂ext V . We let µξV be the Ising probability measure on
ΩV := {−1, +1}V with boundary condition ξ (see the appendix for the definition
of this measure). We let ⟨·⟩ξV denote the corresponding expectation. Moreover, if




                                            7
ξ ≡ +1, we let µξV = µ+                      ξ    −                       ξ    ∅
                      V , if ξ ≡ −1, we let µV = µV and if ξ ≡ 0, we let µV = µV
          ∅
(so µn = µΛn ).
    We refer for instance to [FV17] for a proof of the following three properties.
Recall that we have fixed a finite subset V ⊂ T. We say that a function f : ΩV → R
is increasing if f (η ′ ) ≥ f (η) for every η, η ′ such that η ′ (x) ≥ η(x) for every x ∈ V .

FKG inequality. For any increasing functions f, g : ΩV → R and any boundary
condition ξ ∈ {−1, 0, +1}∂ext V ,

                                     ⟨f g⟩ξV ≥ ⟨f ⟩ξV ⟨g⟩ξV .                        (FKG)

Comparison between boundary conditions. Let ξ, ψ ∈ {−1, 0, +1}∂ext V
be two boundary conditions on V such that ψ(x) ≥ ξ(x) for every x ∈ ∂ext V . For
any increasing function f : ΩV → R,

                                        ⟨f ⟩ψ       ξ
                                            V ≥ ⟨f ⟩V .                             (MON)

Spatial Markov property. Let W ⊆ V , let ξ ∈ {−1, 0, +1}∂ext V be a bound-
ary condition on V and let η ∈ {−1, +1}V \W . Moreover, let ψ ∈ {−1, 0, +1}∂ext W
be the boundary condition on W that coincides with ξ in ∂ext W ∩ ∂ext V and with
η in (∂ext W ) ∩ V . We have

      µξV (spin config. in W = · | spin config. in V \ W equals η) = µψ
                                                                      W.             (SMP)

2.1.2    Percolation properties
In this section, we state two key percolation properties for the (static) Ising model
at inverse temperature β ≤ βc or β < βc . These two properties are not new and are
proven for completeness in the appendix. If 1 ≤ m ≤ n, we consider the elongated
rhombus Λm,n = {k + ℓeiπ/3 : k ∈ {−m, . . . , m}, ℓ ∈ {−n, . . . , n}}. Moreover, we
let Crossm,n denote the left-right crossing event of Λm,n by +1 spins (so Crossn,n =
Crossn ).

Box crossing property. Let β ≤ βc . Then, for every ρ > 0 and δ > 0, there
exists cρ,δ > 0 such that, for every n ≥ (1/ρ) ∨ 1,

                                µ−(δ) (Crossρn,n ) ≥ cρ,δ ,                          (BXP)
                                    Λρn,n

         (δ)
where Λρn,n is the thickened elongated rhombus Λ(1+δ)ρn,(1+δ)n .

Upper bound on the ‘exponent’ of the 4-arm event. Let β < βc and
recall that αn is the µ2n -probability of the 4-arm event from the origin o to ∂Λn .
There exists c > 0 such that, for every n ≥ m ≥ 1,
                                      αn    m 2−c

2.1.3    Spatial mixing property
The first brick in the proof of the spatial mixing property for the pair (σ, σt ) at
β ≤ βc is the analogous static property, that we state now. We do not write the
proof of this property because it is exactly the same as the analogous result for
FK percolation, see for instance [DST17, Theorem 5] and [DM22, Corollary 2.10]
(Remark: the proof is based on (BXP), (SMP) and (MON)).

Spatial mixing. Let β ≤ βc and δ > 0. There exist cδ , Cδ > 0 such that the
                                                                (δ)
following holds for every rhombus Λ. Let A ⊆ {−1, +1}Λ that depends only on
Λ and let ξ and ψ be two boundary conditions on the thickened rhombus Λ(δ) , i.e.
                        (δ)
ξ, ψ ∈ {−1, 0, +1}∂ext Λ . Then,

                       cδ · µψ
                             Λ(δ)
                                  (A) ≤ µξΛ(δ) (A) ≤ Cδ · µψ
                                                           Λ(δ)
                                                                (A).                 (2)
This result (together with the spatial Markov property (SMP)) has the following
two consequences, which are the results that we will use in the present paper. Let
β ≤ βc .
   • For every δ > 0, there exist cδ , Cδ > 0 such that the following holds for every
     n ≥ 1. Let Λ be a rhombus such that the thickened rhombus Λ(δ) is included
     in Λn , let A ⊆ Ωn be a static event that depends only on Λ and let B ⊆ Ωn
     be a static event that depends only on Λn \ Λ(δ) . Then,
                     cδ · µn (A ∩ B) ≤ µn (A)µn (B) ≤ Cδ · µn (A ∩ B).               (3)

   • For every m ≥ 1, η ∈ {−1, +1}Λ2m (x) and x ∈ T, we let T−x η = η(x+·) ∈ Ω2m .
     The second consequence of (2) is the following: There exist c, C > 0 such that
     the following holds for every n ≥ m ≥ 1. Let x ∈ T such that Λm (x) ⊆ Λn .
     Then, for every static event A ⊆ Ω2m that depends only on Λ1.5m , we have
                           c · µ2m (A) ≤ µ2n (Tx A) ≤ C · µ2m (A),                   (4)
      where Tx A is the event A translated by x i.e. Tx A = {η ∈ Ω2n : T−x (η|Λ2m (x) ) ∈
      A}.

2.2     Background on Glauber dynamics
Let n ≥ 1 and β ∈ (0, +∞). In all this section, (σs )s≥0 is the Glauber dynamics in
Λn (from Definition 1.8) at inverse temperature β that starts from σ ∼ µn = µn,β .

2.2.1    Semi-group and infinitesimal generator

formula. Let f : Ωn → R. Then for every t ≥ 0, Pt f : Ωn → R is the function

       2.2.2       A general differential formula
       The strategy proposed in [TV23] to prove noise sensitivity properties is based on
       the study of (integro-)differential inequalities satisfied by (n, t) 7→ πn (t). As a first
       step, let us state a general differential formula for t 7→ E[f (σ)g(σt )] (that is not
       new; this can be seen as a particular case of general differential formulas for Markov
       semi-groups, see e.g. [BGL13]). For completeness, we prove this formula in the
       appendix (Section A.3.2). To state the differential formula in question, we introduce
                               (x)
       a dynamical process (σs )s≥0 for every x ∈ Λn . This dynamical process is defined
       almost exactly like (σs )s≥0 : it is defined on the same probability space, by using
       the same Poisson clocks Yy , the same uniforms Uy,i and the same rates cy (see
       Definition 1.8), but by flipping the spin at x at time 0 (i.e. by starting from the
       configuration σ x instead of σ).

     This last property comes from the fact that, if one starts the Glauber dynamics with two different
initial values η, η ′ ∈ Ωn such that η ′ (x) ≥ η(x) for every x ∈ Λn and uses the same Poisson clocks Yx
and uniforms Ux,i in both cases, then the monotonicity between the two configuration is conserved in
time. To show this last fact, one can use that η ∈ Ωn 7→ cx (η x←− ) is increasing and η ∈ Ωn 7→ cx (η x←+ )
is decreasing where, for every x ∈ Λn and η ∈ Ωn , η x←± is the spin configuration that is obtained from
η by assigning the value ±1 to the spin at x.

      We will need the following dynamical FKG inequality.

      Dynamical FKG. Let F, G : (Ωn )2 → R be two increasing functions.5 Then,
      for any t ≥ 0,                                                     

      Proof. This property is for instance a consequence of [Lig85, Corollary 2.21 of Chap-

      we have
                                        L(f g) ≥ f Lg + gLf.
      Let f and g be two such functions and let η ∈ Ωn . Recall that η x is obtained from η
      by flipping the spin at x. By the formula for L stated in Section 2.2.1, the function
      L(f g) − f Lg − gLf evaluated at η equals

      Remark 2.2. We will actually use the dynamical FKG inequality for a Glauber
      dynamics with general boundary conditions. Let V be a finite subset of T, let ξ be a
      boundary condition on V (i.e. ξ ∈ {−1, 0, +1}∂ext V ) and let (σtξ )t≥0 be a Glauber dy-
      namics in V with boundary condition ξ that starts from a random spin configuration
      σ ξ ∼ µξV (recall that µξV is the Ising measure on V with boundary condition ξ). This
      dynamics is defined exactly like in Definition 1.8 but by replacing the state space
      Ωn by ΩV = {−1, +1}V and the rates cx by cξx (η) := µξV (η x )/(µξV (η) + µξV (η x )).
          The dynamical FKG inequality holds for this dynamics (and the proof is exactly
      the same): for any increasing functions F, G : (ΩV )2 → R and any t ≥ 0,

                          E F (σ ξ , σtξ )G(σ ξ , σtξ ) ≥ E F (σ ξ , σtξ ) E G(σ ξ , σtξ ) .

      2.2.4       Dynamical mixing
      The relaxation time is less than a constant if β < βc . Assume that
      β < βc . Then, there exists c > 0 such that, for any n ≥ 1 and any static event
      A ⊆ Ωn ,
                                P(σ, σt ∈ A) − µn (A)2 ≤ e−ct .                   (5)
      This is proven in [MOS94, Theorme 3.2] under the assumption that the model
      satisfies what is called ‘Strong Mixing Condition for boxes’ (condition (ii) from this
      theorem). This condition can be proven for any β < βc for instance by using the
      coupling with FK percolation as at the end of Section A.2.1.
5
    Saying that F is increasing means that both F (η, ·) and F (·, η) are increasing for every η ∈ Ωn .



                                                         11
      3     Finite-energy for the pair (σ, σt ) for general β
      Static Ising model at positive temperature satisfies a finite-energy property: the cost
      of a local modification is bounded away from 0 and 1 independently of the size n of
      the system. The main goal of this section is to establish a finite-energy property in
      the dynamical setting: at a fixed positive time t > 0, we will also be able to perform
      local modifications on the pair (σ, σt ).

      3.1      Definition of the time and finite-energy constants
      Fix β > 0. In this section we define two constants that will play an important role
      in the rest of the paper: a time constant τ = τ (β) > 0, and a finite-energy constant
      cFE = cFE (β) > 0.

      Definition of the finite-energy constant. In this paragraph, we introduce
      a constant cFE = cFE (β) that will allow us to estimate the costs of local modifications
      on the pair (σ, σt ) (via Proposition 3.2 and Corollary 3.5). Let a = a(β) > 0 be the
      largest constant such that the transition rates cx (as defined in Section 1.5) satisfy

                          ∀n ≥ 1    ∀η ∈ Ωn      ∀x ∈ Λn        cx (η) ∈ [a, 1 − a].           (6)

      We let
                                                        a14
                                              cFE =         .
                                                        16

      Definition of the time constant. Most of our analysis will be carried out for
      some arbitrary but sufficiently small time. For instance, we establish our differential
      formula in Section 4 and the spatial mixing property in Section 5 when the time
      satisfies t ≤ τ . The analysis is much simpler in this perturbative regime because we
      have a good control on the range of interactions induced by the dynamics. In this
      paragraph, we define the time constant τ .
          Consider site percolation on the triangular lattice and let C be the union of the
      cluster of the origin o ∈ T and of the clusters of the neighbours of o. The number
      of connected subsets of T of size k containing o is at most N k for some N > 0.6 . As
      a result, we can (and we do) choose some absolute constant M > 0 such that

             ∀k ≥ 0     {C ⊂ T : |C| = k and C is a possible outcome for C} ≤ M k .

       3.2     Dynamical finite-energy property
       Fix β > 0, and let τ and cFE be as defined in the previous section. In all this
       section, we also fix some n ≥ 1 and consider the Glauber dynamics (σs )s≥0 in Λn
       (from Definition 1.8) starting from σ ∼ µn = µn,β . We are interested in the finite-
       energy properties of the pair (σ, σt ), seen as a random element of the hypercube
       {−1, +1}Λn × {−1, +1}Λn . We refer to σ and σt as the first and second component
       respectively. A difficulty is that the finite-energy cost depends on the time t: if t = 0,
       we must have σt (x) = σ(x) and therefore, we cannot only modify one component at a
       site. If t > 0, changing a configuration where σt (x) = σ(x) to a configuration where
       σt (x) ̸= σ(x) costs at least t because the clock at x must ring at least once. Our first
       result (Proposition 3.2) states that t is, up to constants, the right cost to pay for
       such modification. In our applications, we will use the finite-energy simultaneously
       on both components (we allocate the same spin value at a site at time 0 and at time
       t). In this case, the finite-energy cost is independent of t, see Corollary 3.5. For
       η ∈ Ωn and x ∈ Λn , recall that η x denotes the configuration obtained from η by
       flipping the spin at x.
       Proposition 3.2. For every t ∈ [0, τ ], x ∈ Λn , and η, ψ ∈ Ωn , we have
                                             √
                      P(σ = η, σt = ψ x ) ≥ cFE · tδ · P(σ = η, σt = ψ),

       where δ = ψ(x)η(x) ∈ {−1, 1}.
       Remark 3.3. By reversibility, we can also modify the first coordinate. With the
       same notation as above we also have
                                            √
                       P(σ = η x , σt = ψ) ≥ cFE · tδ · P(σ = η, σt = ψ).         (10)

       Remark 3.4. Proposition 3.2 is stated for t ∈ [0, τ ], and this is what we will use
       in the present paper; but let us observe that the proposition implies a finite-energy
       property at any time. Indeed, by conditioning on σt−τ when t ≥ τ , we obtain the
       following result (where τ appears because it equals τ ∧ (1/τ )): Let η, ψ ∈ Ωn . Then,
       for any t ≥ τ , any x ∈ Λn and any η, ψ ∈ Ωn ,
                                               √
                          P(σ = η, σt = ψ x ) ≥ cFE · τ · P(σ = η, σt = ψ).

       A general sketch of proof. Before writing the proof of Proposition 3.2, let
       us write a sketch of proof for this result, that will also be useful in order to read
       the proofs of the other ‘general’ properties of the pair (σ, σt ) proven in Sections 3–
       5. As explained in Section 1.4, the main difficulty is that, contrary to the static
       configuration σ, the pair (σ, σt ) does not satisfy the spatial Markov property.7
   7
     Let us be a little more precise: the spatial Markov property for the pair would be the property that
for any V ⊆ Λn , the law of (σ, σt )|V conditionally on (σ, σt )|Λn \V is the same as if we just condition on


                                                        13
          In order to overcome this, given some site x, we will define a random set contain-
      ing x such that some relevant information (for instance, the fact that the clocks have
      rung or not) in the interior of this set is independent of the exterior of it. This set
      will be the ‘red cluster’ of x (and of its neighbours) in the proof of Proposition 3.2.
      In Sections 4 and 5, it will be the ‘green cluster’ of x (and of its neighbours). This
      independence property can be seen as a weak spatial Markov property.
          As an example of such an independence property, the reader can have in mind
      that if we fix a circuit γ and we condition on σ|γ and on the the event that the clocks
      in γ have not rung before some fixed time t, then (if we consider only the dynamics
      until time t) the dynamical process in the region surrounded by γ is independent of
      the dynamical process outside this region.
          In Sections 3 and 4, we essentially prove that these random ‘red’ and ‘green’
      clusters are typically small. Roughly speaking, this means that the information of
      the value of the spin at x travels very slowly, which helps to prove finite-energy and
      spatial mixing properties. The finite-energy property of the static Ising model will
      be the key tool to prove that the ‘red’ clusters are small (or more precisely that the
      cost of making them large is always greater than the cost of assigning the desired
      values to x, see (11) below), which will enable us to prove the finite-energy property
      of the pair (σ, σt ), i.e. Proposition 3.2. Then, the finite-energy property of the pair
      will be they key tool to prove that the ‘green’ clusters are small, see Sections 4.1
      and 4.2 (in particular Lemmas 4.5 and 4.6). Once we know that the green clusters
      are small, we can prove several properties of the pair (σ, σt ), see Section 4.3 and
      Section 5. In particular, in Section 5.1, we use this in order to transfer the spatial
      mixing property of the static Ising model to the pair (σ, σt ) (when β ≤ βc ).

      Proof of Proposition 3.2. Fix two spin configurations η, ψ ∈ Ωn , some x ∈ Λn and a
      time t ∈ [0, τ ]. Moreover, let D = {z ∈ Λn : η(z) ̸= ψ(z)} denote the (deterministic)
      disagreement set of η and ψ, and D′ = D∆{x} be the disagreement set of η and ψ x .
          We call red sites all sites in Λn whose clock has rung more than necessary for
      the event {σ = η, σt = ψ} to hold. More precisely, any z ∈ Λn \ D is red if its clock
      has rung at least once between times 0 and t and any z ∈ D is red if its clock has
      rung at least twice between times 0 and t. We let R be the set of red sites and
      Rx denote the union of the red component of x and of the red components of the
      neighbours of x (Remark: By convention, if a site is not red then its red component
      is the empty set. In particular, Rx = ∅ means that x is not red and has no red
      neighbour). Our goal is to prove the following statement:
                                                                     |R|+1
                                                     |R|−δ       2
        ∀R ⊆ Λn     P(σ = η, σt = ψ, Rx = R) ≤ t                               P(σ = η, σt = ψ x ), (11)
                                                                 a7

    We now discuss the cost of a ‘synchronized’ finite modification, where we allocate

                  P(σ = η x←s , σt = ψ x←s ) ≥ cFE · P(σ = η, σt = ψ).

4     The events {σ, σt ∈ A} for general β
In this section, we start our analysis of the events {σ, σt ∈ A} by using the finite-
energy property of the previous section. In particular, we prove that we can intersect
these events with a ‘decoupling event’ without changing much its probability (see
Section 4.2) and we prove a differential inequality for t 7→ P(σ, σt ∈ A) in terms of
pivotal events (see Section 4.3).
    Fix β > 0. Let cFE and τ be the constants as defined in Section 3.1. In all this
section, we also fix some n ≥ 1 and consider the Glauber dynamics (σs )s≥0 in Λn
(from Definition 1.8) that starts from σ ∼ µn = µn,β .
    Recall that in this paper a static event is just a subset of Ωn = {−1, 1}Λn .


                                              16
4.1    A Cauchy–Schwarz trick
We start with a rather elementary ‘trick’ that we will use both in the proof of
‘general’ results about the events {σ, σt ∈ A} (in Sections 4 and 5) and in the
percolation sections of the paper.
Lemma 4.1. Let A, B ⊆ Ωn . For every t ≥ 0,
                                   
           P(σ ∈ A, σt ∈ B) ≤ max P(σ, σt ∈ A), P(σ, σt ∈ B) .

Proof. By the Markov property, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and then reversibil-
ity, we have
                              h                          i
          P(σ ∈ A, σt ∈ B) = E P σ ∈ A σt/2 P σt ∈ B σt/2
                             r h
                                             2 i h              2 i
                           ≤ E P σ ∈ A σt/2 E P σt ∈ B σt/2
                             p
                           = P(σ, σt ∈ A)P(σ, σt ∈ B).

   Let us now state and prove a lemma that is a consequence of the finite-energy
property and the Cauchy–Schwarz trick.

Definition of the green set. Recall that the Glauber dynamics (σs )s≥0 is
defined by sampling an initial configuration σ and then updating it by using the
Poisson clocks Yx and the uniform variables Ux,i (see Definition 1.8). We call green
sites all sites in Λn whose clock has rung before time τ , we let G be the set of green
sites and, for every x ∈ Λn and we let Gx denote the union of the green component
of x and of the green components of the neighbours of x (Remark: By convention, if
a site is not green then its green component is the empty set. In particular, Gx = ∅
means that x is not green and has no green neighbour). If H ⊆ Λn , η ∈ Ωn and
α ∈ {−1, +1}H , we let α|η be the spin configuration that coincides with α on H
and with η in Λn \ H. Moreover, we let

                              Aα = {η ∈ Ωn : α|η ∈ A}.

(If the reader wants motivation before reading the proof of the following lemma,
they can first read Section 4.2.)
Lemma 4.2. Let x ∈ Λn , G ⊆ Λn and A, B ⊆ Ωn . Let H = G ∪ {x}. Then, for
every t ∈ [0, τ ],

                 P σ ∈ Aα , σt ∈ Bβ , Gx = G

                                                 · τ |G| · max P σ, σt ∈ A , P σ, σt ∈ B .
                                                                                      
                          ≤
                                  cFE

Proof. Let x, G, A, B, H, t as in the statement and let α, β ∈ {−1, +1}H . Recall
that ∂ext H = {y ∈ T \ H : ∃x ∈ H, x ∼ y}. In this proof, we will intersect ∂ext H
with G, which is a subset of Λn , so when the reader thinks of ∂ext H, they may have
{y ∈ Λn \ H : ∃x ∈ H, x ∼ y} in mind.


                                                 17
    We note that the event {Gx = G} is included in the event {G ⊆ G, ∂ext H ∩
G = ∅}. An observation concerning the green set that compensates for the lack
of spatial Markov property for the pair (σ, σt ) is that the event {∂ext H ∩ G =
∅, σ ∈ Aα , σt ∈ Bβ } is measurable with respect to the initial configuration σ and all
the Poisson clocks and uniforms outside H (because in this event the spins at the
exterior boundary of H have not been updated). In particular, it is independent of
the Poisson clocks in H. This independence property gives

P σ ∈ Aα , σt ∈ Bβ , Gx = G ≤ τ |G| P ∂ext G ∩ G = ∅, σ ∈ Aα , σt ∈ Bβ
                                                                       

                               ≤ τ |G| P σ ∈ Aα , σt ∈ Bβ
                                                          

                               ≤ τ |G| max P(σ, σt ∈ Aα ), P(σ, σt ∈ Bβ ) by Lem. 4.1.
                                           



The following claim implies the desired result by summing on every α, β.
Claim 4.3. We have

                      P(σ, σt ∈ Aα ) ≤                    · P(σ, σt ∈ A).

Proof of the claim. By induction, it is sufficient to prove the result when H is a

from η by assigning the value s to the spin at y and let As = {η ∈ Ωn : η y←s ∈ A}.
Our goal is to prove that P(σ, σt ∈ As ) ≤ (4/cFE ) · P(σ, σt ∈ A). By Corollary 3.5,
we have

   This ends the proof of the lemma.

4.2    The decoupling event
In this section, we prove a decoupling result that will imply spatial mixing when

definition. Recall the notation Gx from Section 4.1.
Definition 4.4. Given a non-empty set S ⊆ Λn , we define the decoupling event
dec(S) as follows:               \
                        dec(S) =     |Gx | ≤ log |S| .

4.3    Differentiation
In this section, we prove that the interpretation of the differential formulas in terms
of pivotal events – that is true in the case of Bernoulli percolation under i.i.d.
dynamics (see e.g. [TV23, Prop. 4.2]) – still holds in the case of the Ising model (up
to a multiplicative constant and at times t ≤ τ ).
Definition 4.7. Let W ⊆ Λn , A ⊆ Ωn and η ∈ Ωn . We say that W is pivotal
for A ⊆ Ωn in η if there exists ψ ∈ Ωn such that η and ψ coincide outside W and
1A (ψ) ̸= 1A (η). If {x} is pivotal for A in η, we simply say that x is pivotal for A in
η. We let Pivx (A) ⊆ Ωn denote the event that x is pivotal for A.

5     The events {σ, σt ∈ A} for β ≤ βc
Fix β ≤ βc . Let cFE and τ be the constants as defined in Section 3.1. Recall that
in this paper a static event is just a subset of Ωn .

5.1     Spatial mixing
In all this section, we fix some n ≥ 1 and we let (σs )s≥0 be the Glauber dynamics in
Λn (from Definition 1.8) that starts from σ ∼ µn = µn,β . In this section, we prove a
spatial mixing result for events of the form {σ, σt ∈ A}. As in Section 1.2, we write
Λ(δ) for the (1 + δ)-blown-up version of a rhombus Λ.
Proposition 5.1. For every δ > 0, there exist two constants cδ , Cδ > 0 that do not
depend on n such that the following holds. Let Λ be a rhombus such that Λ(δ) ⊆ Λn
and let A and B be two static events. If A depends only on Λ and B depends only
on Λn \ Λ(δ) , then for every t ∈ [0, τ ],
        cδ P(σ, σt ∈ A ∩ B) ≤ P(σ, σt ∈ A)P(σ, σt ∈ B) ≤ Cδ P(σ, σt ∈ A ∩ B).


                                           21
   Our proof of Proposition 5.1 is based on Lemma 4.5 and on another lemma that
we state and prove now. Recall that the Glauber dynamics is defined by using the
Poisson clocks Yx and the uniforms Ux,i , see Definition 1.8.
Lemma 5.2. For every δ > 0, there exist cδ , Cδ > 0 that do not depend on n
such that the following holds. Let Λ be a rhombus such that Λ(δ) ⊆ Λn , let A be
a dynamical event measurable with respect to (σ, Y, U )|Λ and let B be a dynamical
event measurable with respect to (σ, Y, U )|Λn \Λ(δ) . Then,

                       cδ P(A ∩ B) ≤ P(A)P(B) ≤ Cδ P(A ∩ B).

Proof. In this proof, we use the symbol ≍δ to denote the same thing as ≍ but
with constants that may depend on δ. To prove the claim, we are going to use the
analogous result for the static Ising model (stated in Section 2.1.3). By writing 1A
as a function of (σ, Y, U )|Λ and 1B as a function of (σ, Y, U )|Λn \Λ(δ) , we have
                                  
   P(A ∩ B) = E P A ∩ B Y, U
                    h                     i
             ≍δ E P A Y, U P B Y, U             by (3) and since σ indep. of (Y, U )
                  h                                   i
             = E P A (Y, U )|Λ P B (Y, U )|Λn \Λ(δ)
             = P(A)P(B),

where is the two last equalities we have used that σ, (Y, U )|Λ and (Y, U )|Λn \Λ(δ) are
independent.
   We can now prove Proposition 5.1. Below, given a rhombus Λ, we let dec =
dec(∂Λ) and dec(δ) = dec(∂(Λ(δ) )). (Recall the notation dec(S) from Definition 4.4.)
Proof of Proposition 5.1. Let δ > 0, t ∈ [0, τ ] and let Λ be a rhombus such that
Λ(δ) ⊆ Λn . Let A, B as in the statement. The proof is based on the observation that,
if the sides of Λ are larger than some Mδ > 0 (that we fix), then {σ, σt ∈ A} ∩ dec is
measurable with respect to (σ, Y, U ) restricted to Λ(δ/4) . This comes from the fact
that, on dec, there is a circuit made of non-green sites that is included in Λ(δ/4) and
surrounds Λ. Similarly, {σ, σt ∈ B} ∩ dec(δ) is measurable with respect to (σ, Y, U )
restricted to Λn \ Λ(δ/2) . Let us assume – as a first step – that the sides of Λ are
indeed larger than Mδ . Then, Lemma 5.2 gives

                    P {σ, σt ∈ A} ∩ dec · P {σ, σt ∈ B} ∩ dec(δ)
                                                                 

                    ≍δ P {σ, σt ∈ A} ∩ dec ∩ {σ, σt ∈ B} ∩ dec(δ) ,
                                                                    

where the symbol ≍δ denotes the same thing as ≍ but with constants that may
depend on δ. We conclude by applying Lemma 4.5 three times (to S = ∂Λ, S =
∂(Λ(δ) ) and S=∂Λ ∪ ∂Λ(δ) ; N.B: we use that dec ∩ dec(δ) ⊆ dec(∂Λ ∪ ∂Λ(δ) )).
   It remains to prove the result when the sides of Λ are less than Mδ , which we
now assume. We also assume that A is non-empty (otherwise the result is trivial).
We obtain the left-hand-side of the inequality by writing

          P(σ, σt ∈ A)P(σ, σt ∩ B) ≥ c0 P(σ, σt ∈ B) ≥ c0 P(σ, σt ∈ A ∩ B),

where c0 = minE⊆Ωn that dep. only on Λ µn (E)2 (Remark: we have used that, as men-
tioned at the end of Section 2.2.1, P(σ, σt ∈ A) ≥ µn (A)2 ).


                                          22
    We prove the right-hand-side of the inequality by using the finite energy property
for the pair (σ, σt ). More precisely, we first fix some α ∈ {−1, +1}Λ such that
η|Λ = α ⇒ η ∈ A. If ψ ∈ {−1, +1}Λn \Λ , we let α|ψ be the spin configuration that
coincides with α in Λ and with ψ in Λn \ Λ. Moreover, we let B ′ = {η|(Λn \Λ) : η ∈
B} ⊆ {−1, +1}Λn \Λ . We have
                       X
  P(σ, σt ∈ A ∩ B) ≥        P(σ = α|ψ, σt = α|ψ ′ )
                       ψ,ψ ′ ∈B ′
                         1          X            X
                   =                                       P(σ = α|ψ, σt = α|ψ ′ )
                       4|Λ|
                              β,β ′ ∈{−1,+1}Λ ψ,ψ ′ ∈B ′
                        |Λ|
                       cFE          X            X
                   ≥                                       P(σ = β|ψ, σt = β ′ |ψ ′ )   by Cor. 3.5
                       4|Λ|
                              β,β ′ ∈{−1,+1}Λ ψ,ψ ′ ∈B ′
                        |Λ|                       |Λ|
                       cFE                c
                   =    |Λ|
                            P(σ, σt ∈ B) ≥ FE  P(σ, σt ∈ A)P(σ, σt ∈ B).
                       4                  4|Λ|
This concludes the proof.

   We will also need to decouple an event measurable with respect to (σ, σt ) and
an event measurable with respect to σ. More precisely, we will need the following
proposition.
Proposition 5.3. For every δ > 0, there exist two constants cδ , Cδ > 0 that do not
depend on n such that the following holds. Let Λ be a rhombus such that Λ(δ) ⊆ Λn
and let A and B be two static events. If A depends only on Λ and B depends only
on Λn \ Λ(δ) , then for any t ∈ [0, τ ],

      cδ P(σ ∈ A, σ, σt ∈ B) ≤ P(σ ∈ A)P(σ, σt ∈ B) ≤ Cδ P(σ ∈ A, σ, σt ∈ B)

and

      cδ P(σ, σt ∈ A, σ ∈ B) ≤ P(σ, σt ∈ A)P(σ ∈ B) ≤ Cδ P(σ, σt ∈ A, σ ∈ B).

Proof. Let us prove the second estimate. The proof of the first one is the same. As
in the proof of Proposition 5.1, we notice that it the sides of Λ are large enough,
then Lemma 5.2 implies that
                                           
                       P {σ, σt ∈ A} ∩ dec P(σ ∈ B)
                                                          
                        ≍δ P {σ, σt ∈ A} ∩ dec ∩ {σ ∈ B} .

Again as in the proof of Proposition 5.1, we conclude by applying Lemma 4.5 and if
the sides of Λ are less than some constant then we conclude by applying Corollary 3.5
to every x ∈ Λ.

5.2    Combining spatial mixing and FKG inequality
As in the previous section, we fix some n ≥ 1 and we let (σs )s≥0 be the Glauber
dynamics in Λn (from Definition 1.8) that starts from σ ∼ µn = µn,β . (Recall that
for all of Section 5 we have fixed some β ≤ βc .) By the dynamical FKG inequality
(see Section 2.2.3), two increasing events measurable with respect to the pair (σ, σt )


                                                 23
are positively correlated. However, we will sometimes need to use that two events
correlate well even if they are not both increasing everywhere. In practice, we will
use the following proposition, whose proof is close to that of the spatial mixing
property Proposition 5.4 (and also relies on the dynamical FKG inequality). We
say that a static event A ⊆ Ωn is increasing in some set V ⊆ Λn if 1A (ψ) ≥ 1A (η)
for every spin configurations η, ψ ∈ Ωn such that ψ coincides with η in Λn \ V and
ψ(x) ≥ η(x) for every x ∈ V .
Proposition 5.4. For every δ > 0, there exist two constants cδ , Cδ > 0 that do not
depend on n such that the following holds. Let Λ be a rhombus such that Λ(δ) ⊆ Λn
and let A and B be two static events. If A is increasing and depends only on Λ and
B is increasing in Λ(δ) , then for every t ∈ [0, τ ],

                    P(σ, σt ∈ A ∩ B) ≥ cδ P(σ, σt ∈ A)P(σ, σt ∈ B).

Proof. Let δ > 0 and let Λ be a rhombus such that Λ(δ) ⊆ Λn . We first observe that
if the sides of Λ are less than some constant then the proposition is a consequence
of Corollary 3.5 (applied to every x ∈ Λ – like in the proof of Proposition 5.1), so
we assume that these sides are larger than some Mδ > 0 that we will fix during the
proof. We define dec(δ) and dec as in the previous section, i.e. dec = dec(∂Λ) and
dec(δ) = dec(∂(Λ(δ) )). Moreover, we let Γ be the outermost circuit in Λ(δ) \ Λ(δ/2)
that surrounds Λ(δ/2) and is made of non-green sites (recall that a green site is a site
whose clock has rung before time τ ). This circuit exists on the event dec(δ) as soon
as Mδ is large enough, which we assume. If this circuit does not exist, we let Γ = ∅
(this is a convention that has no importance). If γ is a circuit that surrounds Λ(δ/2) ,
we let γout denote the union of γ and of all the points of Λn that are separated from
Λ(δ/2) by γ (and we use the convention γout = Λn if γ = ∅). We have
                                 h                                 i
            P(σ, σt ∈ A ∩ B) = E P σ, σt ∈ A ∩ B Γ, (σ, σt )|Γout
                                 h                                        i
                              ≥ E P σ, σt ∈ A ∩ B Γ, (σ, σt )|Γout 1{Γ̸=∅} .       (16)

Let γ and (η, ψ) be possible values for Γ and (σ, σt )|Γout respectively, with γ ̸= ∅,
and let                                 
                    Eγ,η,ψ = {Γ = γ} ∩ (σ, σt )|Γout = (η, ψ) .
We claim that we have the following due to the spatial Markov property of the static
Ising model: Let γint = Λn \γout be the region surrounded by γ. Then, conditionally
on Eγ,η,ψ , the law of (σs )s∈[0,τ ] in γint is that of the Glauber dynamics in this set
with boundary conditions given by η|γ , and starting from its invariant probability
measure.
    To prove this claim, we first observe that it is true if we rather condition on the
         ′
event Eγ,η,ψ    that σ coincides with η in γ and that no clock in γ has rung before
                                                    ′
time τ . The event Eγ,η,ψ equals the event Eγ,η,ψ         intersected with an event of the
                                                                           ′
σ-algebra generated (σ, Y, U )|γout . Moreover, conditionally on Eγ,η,ψ        , the process
(σs )s∈[0,τ ] in γint is independent of (σ, Y, U )|γout . As a result, the law of (σs )s∈[0,τ ]
                                                                         ′
in γint conditionally on Eγ,η,ψ is the same as conditionally on Eγ,η,ψ        . This proves
the claim.
    We are now going to apply the dynamical FKG inequality stated in Section 2.2.3:
by the claim just above and the dynamical FKG inequality for the Glauber dynamics


                                              24
       in γint with boundary conditions given by η|γ (see Remark 2.2), we have9
                                                                            
             P σ, σt ∈ A ∩ B Eγ,η,ψ ≥ P σ, σt ∈ A Eγ,η,ψ P σ, σt ∈ B Eγ,η,ψ .                       (17)

           Now, we are going to erase the conditioning in the first term of the right-hand-
       side of (17). We observe that, if Mδ large enough – which we assume –, then the
       event {σ, σt ∈ A} ∩ dec is measurable with respect to (σ, Y, U ) restricted to Λ(δ/4) .
       Moreover, Eγ,η,ψ is measurable with respect to (σ, Y, U ) restricted to the complement
       of Λ(δ/2) . As a result (by using Lemma 5.2 in the second inequality), there exists a
       constant cδ > 0 such that
                                                                              
                                            P {σ, σt ∈ A} ∩ dec ∩ Eγ,η,ψ
                        P σ, σt ∈ A Eγ,η,ψ ≥                       
                                                         P Eγ,η,ψ
                                                                       
                                            ≥ cδ P {σ, σt ∈ A} ∩ dec .                    (18)

       By combining (16), (17) and (18), we obtain that
                                                                                 
             P σ, σt ∈ A ∩ B ≥ cδ P {σ, σt ∈ A} ∩ dec · P {σ, σt ∈ B} ∩ {Γ ̸= ∅}
                               ≥ cδ P {σ, σt ∈ A} ∩ dec · P {σ, σt ∈ B} ∩ dec(δ) .
                                                                               

       We conclude by applying Lemma 4.5.

       5.3     Quasi-invariance by translation
       As explained at the end of Section 1.2, since we work in finite volume, we do not have
       translation invariance but we rather have a quasi-invariance by translation property
       that we state and prove now. Note that in the following statement, contrary to the
       previous sections, (σs )s≥0 is the Glauber dynamics in Λ2n starting from σ ∼ µ2n
       (so we work in Λ2n rather than Λn ). Recall that if m ≥ 1, η ∈ {−1, 1}Λ2m (x) and
       x ∈ T, we let T−x η = η(x + ·) ∈ Ω2m .
       Proposition 5.5. There exist c, C > 0 such that the following holds. Let n ≥ m ≥ 1,
       let (σs )s≥0 be the Glauber dynamics in Λ2n starting from σ ∼ µ2n and let (σs′ )s≥0
       denote the Glauber dynamics in Λ2m starting from σ ′ ∼ µ2m . Moreover, let A ⊆ Ω2m
       be a static event that depends only on Λm and let x ∈ T such that Λm (x) ⊆ Λn .
       Then, for any t ∈ [0, τ ],

                         cP(σ ′ , σt′ ∈ A) ≤ P σ, σt ∈ Tx A ≤ CP(σ ′ , σt′ ∈ A),
                                                           

       where Tx A is the event A translated by x i.e. Tx A = {η ∈ Ω2n : T−x (η|Λ2m (x) ) ∈ A}.

       Proof. Let M > 0 be a constant that we will fix during the proof. We first notice
       that it is sufficient to prove the proposition under the assumption that m is larger
       than M . So let m ≥ M . If f : Ω2m → R, we let Tx f : Ω2n → R be defined by
       Tx f (η) = f (T−x (η|Λ2m (x) )). By spatial mixing of the static Ising model, for every
       function f : Ω2m → R+ that only depends on Λ1.5m we have

                                         E[f (σ ′ )] ≍ E Tx f (σ) .

6     Percolation arguments for β ≤ βc
Fix β ≤ βc for the whole section. Let τ be the time constant as defined in Section 3.1.
   As in [TV23], the following ‘dynamical four-arm probability’ is at the core of our
analysis:                                             
                             πn (t) = P σ, σt ∈ A4 (n) ,
where (σs )s≥0 is the Glauber dynamics in Λ2n starting from σ ∼ µ2n . (Recall that
A4 (n) is the four-arm event defined in Section 1.3.)
    In this section, we prove the quasi-multiplicativity property for πn (t) and the
multiscale analogous quantities πm,n (t) that we define just below. Then, we use this
property and the differential formula Proposition 4.8 to prove differential inequalities
for πn (t) and P(σ, σt ∈ Crossn ).

6.1    Quasi-multiplicativity
The quasi-multiplicativity property is a key tool in the study of arm events. It
was first established by Kesten [Kes87] in the context of Bernoulli percolation,
to prove scaling relations between critical and near-critical exponents. See also
[Wer07, Nol08, SS10, DMT21a] for alternative proofs and additional applications
in this context. For dynamical arm events (i.e. events of the kind {a 4-arm event
holds at times 0 and t}), quasi-multiplicativity was established by Garban, Pete and
Schramm [GPS10] for Bernoulli percolation under i.i.d. dynamics (see also the ap-
pendix of [RT24]). In this section, we prove the analogue of the quasi-multiplicativity
of [GPS10] in the case of the (high temperature) Ising model, following the approach
of [DMT21a, RT24] and combining it with the Cauchy–Schwarz trick (Lemma 4.1).
Definition 6.1. Let n ≥ m ≥ 2. We let A4 (m, n) ⊂ Ω2n denote the event that
there are four paths of alternating signs from ∂Λm to ∂Λn included in the annulus
Λn \ Λm−1 (Remark: We can – and we will – see A4 (m, n) as a subset of ΩN for any
N ≥ n). We let
                                                                     
            αm,n = µ2n (A4 (m, n)) and πm,n (t) = P σ, σt ∈ A4 (m, n) ,

where (σs )s≥0 is the Glauber dynamics in Λ2n starting from σ ∼ µ2n . For n ≥ 1,
we set
                         α1,n = αn and π1,n (t) = πn (t),



                                           26
Proposition 6.2 (Quasi-multliplicativity property). There exist c, C > 0 such that,
for any n ≥ m ≥ k ≥ 1 and t ∈ [0, τ ],

                         cπk,n (t) ≤ πk,m (t)πm,n (t) ≤ Cπk,n (t).

Remark 6.3. By Proposition 6.2 and the box-crossing property, there exists c > 0
such that for every n ≥ m ≥ 2 and t ∈ [0, τ ], πm/2,2n (t) ≥ cπm,n (t).

6.1.1    Separation of arms
The main ingredient in the proof of the quasi-multiplicativity property is the proof
of the so-called separation of arms property.
Definition 6.4. Let n ≥ 100 and let x1 , . . . , x4 denote the centers of the left,
bottom, right and top sides of Λn . We let Asep 4 (m, n) ⊂ A4 (m, n) denote the (static)
event that for every i ∈ {1, . . . , 4} odd (resp. even) there exists a path from ∂Λm
to ∂Λn included in the annulus Λn \ Λm−1 that (a) does not intersect the three
rhombii Λn/10 (xj ), j ̸= i, (b) is only made of +1 (resp. −1) spins and (c) ends on
Λn/20 (xi ) ∩ ∂Λn . Moreover, we let
                              sep
                                  (t) = P σ, σt ∈ Asep
                                                            
                            πm,n                   4 (m, n) ,

where (σs )s≥0 is the Glauber dynamics in Λ2n starting from σ ∼ µ2n .
Proposition 6.5 (Separation of arms). There exists c > 0 such that, for every
m ≥ 1, every n ≥ (4m) ∨ 100 and every t ∈ [0, τ ],
                                    sep
                                   πm,4n (t) ≥ cπm,n (t).

    Roughly speaking, we use standard arguments to deduce the proposition above
from the box-crossing property and the spatial mixing and FKG results Proposi-
tions 5.1 and 5.4. The main new difficulty that was not present in previous ap-
proaches and that we had to overcome is of combinatorial nature. We are consid-
ering 4 arms at time 0 and at time t. When we localize the arms at time 0 and at
time t, there is no reason a priori that the 4 arms land at the same places at both
times, and some combinatorial obstructions may appear. The Cauchy–Schwarz trick
(Lemma 4.1) solves this issue and asserts that the most likely case is when the arms
land roughly at the same place at time 0 and at time t. This is detailed in the proof
of Lemma 6.9. We decompose the proof into three lemmas (Lemmas 6.6, 6.8 and
6.9). The first lemma is concerned with one of the main advantage of separated
arms: since the arms are at macroscopic distance of each other, we can use standard
box-crossing constructions to extend them to a larger scale.
Lemma 6.6. There exists c > 0 such that, for every n, m ≥ 1 that satisfy n ≥
(4m) ∨ 100 and any t ∈ [0, τ ],

          The main idea behind the proof of the separation of arms is that two interfaces
       land typically at macroscopic distance of each other at the boundary of a box.
       Technically, this is due to the fact that two interfaces landing close to each others

                                                      28
Definition 6.7. Given n ≥ 100 and δ ∈ (0, 1/100) such that n ≥ 1/δ, we let
Sepδn ⊂ Ω2n be the static event defined by the fact that there is no x ∈ ∂Λn such
that there exist three paths of alternating sign from ∂Λ16δn (x) to ∂Λn/2 that are
included in Λn (Remark: We can – and we will – see Sepδn as a subset of ΩN for any
N ≥ n).
    We will use two important properties of Sepδn . First, Lemma 6.8 asserts that it
is a typical event: its probability is closed to 1 provided the separation parameter δ
is small enough. Second, its occurrence forces arms to separate at scale n. This is
formally expressed in Claim 6.11 below, and – together with the Cauchy–Schwarz
trick – is the central argument in the proof of Lemma 6.9.
Lemma 6.8. There exists C > 0 such that, for every δ ∈ (0, 1/100) and n ≥ 1/δ,

                                     µ2n (Sepδn ) ≥ 1 − Cδ.

Proof. Let D ⊂ ∂Λn be a subset of size ≍ 1δ such that, each point x ∈ D is at
(Euclidean) distance less than 16δn from the other points of D. We observe that
if Sepδn does not hold then there exits x ∈ D such that a 3-arm event holds in a
half-plane around x from distance 32δn to distance n/2. More precisely, if Sepδn
does not hold then there exists x ∈ D such that there exist three arms of alternating
color included in Λn from ∂Λ32δn (x) to ∂Λn/2 . By using that the exponent of the
3-arm event is (at least) 2 (see Section A.2.2 in the appendix), we obtain that – for
fixed x – the probability of this event is less than a constant times δ 2 . (Remark:
here, we have also used quasi-invariance by translation for the static model, i.e. (4).)
We obtain the desired result by applying the union bound.

   Let us state and prove the third lemma of this subsection.

    Let us finish the proof of the lemma by showing the claim. To this purpose, we are
going to consider the interfaces that cross Λn \Λm . An interface is a continuous path
in R2 that is included on the union of edges of the hexagonal lattice (which is dual
to the triangular lattice) and that has only +1 sites on one of its side and only −1
sites on the other side. If A4 (m, n) holds, then there are at least four interfaces that
are disjoint (in the sense that the continuous paths are disjoint) and that cross this
annulus. Assume that A4 (m, n) holds, let γ1 , . . . , γ4 be four consecutive interfaces
and let z1 , . . . , z4 ∈ ∂Λn be four vertices of the triangular lattice that are adjacent to
the endpoints of γ1 , . . . , γ4 respectively and whose signs are +, −, +, − respectively.
We observe that if Sepδn holds, then for every i ∈ {1 . . . , 4}, γi ∩ ∪j̸=i Λ8δn (zj ) = ∅
                                                                                        

(by this, we mean that the set of sites adjacent to γi does not intersect ∪j̸=i Λ8δn (zj )).
One concludes the proof of the claim by letting xi be the point of Dnδ that is closest
to zi and noting that Aδ,X   4 (m, n) holds, where X = (x1 , . . . , x4 ).

6.2    Differential inequalities for percolation events
In this section, we prove differential inequalities for (dynamical) percolation events
by using the quasi-multiplicativity property Proposition 6.2 and the differential for-
mula Proposition 4.8.

7      Sharp noise sensitivity for β < βc
Fix β < βc for the whole section (N.B: this implies that the ‘exponent’ of the 4-arm
event is less than 2, see (1)). Let τ be the time constant as defined in Section 3.1.
   We now have all the intermediate results needed to adapt the proof of [TV23]
and prove the sharp noise sensitivity theorem (Theorem 1.6). The only difference is
that we have made our analysis only for times t ∈ [0, τ ]. We will use the dynamical
mixing property (see Section 2.2.4) to overcome this (as well as some monotonicity
property in times). Let us finish the proof step by step, but by referring to [TV23]
when there is no difference at all.

7.1     Superquadratic decay above the sensitivity length
As in [TV23], we define the ‘noise sensitivity length’ ℓ(t) as follows:

                           ℓ(t) = min{n ≥ 1 : n2 αn ≥ 1/t}.

We refer to [TV23, Sections 1.2 and 2.1] for more discussions about this quantity.
The general idea is that sharp noise sensitivity means that the percolation events
are sensitive to an amount t of noise at all scales ≫ ℓ(t) but are stable under this
amount of noise at all scales ≪ ℓ(t). This is essentially the content of Theorem 1.6,
which is the main result of the present paper.


                                          34
    In this section, we first notice that we have the following three properties, which
are the analogues of Properties (P1), (P2) and (P3) from [TV23, Section 6]. More
precisely, there exists C > 0 such that
   • For every n ≥ 1 and 0 ≤ t ≤ u ≤ τ ,
                                                    n
                                                 Z uX               !
                            πn (t)
                         1≤        ≤ exp C                  kπk (s)ds ;
                            πn (u)                t   k=1

   • For every n ≥ 1,               Z τ
                                          n2 πn (t)dt ≤ C;
                                     0

   • For every n ≥ m ≥ 1 and 0 ≤ t ≤ u ≤ τ ,

                               πn (u)πm (t) ≤ Cπm (u)πn (t).

Proof. The first and second properties come from Lemmas 6.15 and 6.13 respectively.
The third one is a consequence of the quasi-multiplicativity property Proposition 6.2
and the monotonicity of s 7→ πm,n (s) (see the end of Section 2.2.1):

                        πn (u)                         πn (t)
                               ≍ πm,n (u) ≤ πm,n (t) ≍        .
                        πm (u)                         πm (t)

   The following proposition is the analogue of [TV23, Proposition 6.1], which is
the main intermediate result from [TV23].
Proposition 7.1. There exist c, C > 0 such that, for every t ∈ [0, τ ] and every
n ≥ m ≥ ℓ(t),
                             πn (t)     m 2+c
                                    ≤C          .

Proof. Thanks to the three properties stated just before the proposition (and thanks
to (1)), the proof is exactly the same as in [TV23, Section 6] (Remark: The fact
that the times are less than τ in these three properties does not change anything at
all to the proof).

and εn = 1/(n2 αn ).

A.1     The Ising model with boundary conditions
In this appendix, we recall the definition of the Ising model in a finite set with some
boundary conditions ξ.
Definition A.1. Let V be a finite subset of T, let E(V ) denote the set of edges
whose endpoints are both in V and let ξ be a boundary condition on V , i.e. ξ ∈
{−1, 0, +1}∂ext V . The energy of a configuration η ∈ ΩV := {−1, +1}V is defined by
                             X                      X               
            H ξ (η) = −               η(x)η(y) +             η(x)ξ(y) .
                           {x,y}∈E(V )                    ∈V : x∼y
                                                     x∈V,y /

Given some β ∈ (0, +∞), the Ising measure at inverse temperature β on V with
boundary condition ξ is the probability measure µξV = µξV,β on ΩV defined by

                                           37
      A.2 Static percolation: the box-crossing property and two
      consequences
      A.2.1      The box-crossing property
      In this section, we prove the box-crossing property (BXP), i.e. we prove that if
      β ≤ βc , then for every ρ > 0 and δ > 0, there exists cρ,δ > 0 such that, for every
      n ≥ 1,
                                   µ−(δ) (Crossρn,n ) ≥ cρ,δ ,
                                        Λρn,n
             (δ)
      where Λρn,n is the thickened elongated rhombus Λ(1+δ)ρn,(1+δ)n .
      Proof in the case β = βc . When β = βc , this is a consequence of the coupling be-
      tween the Ising model (with −1 boundary conditions) and the FK–Ising model (with
      wired boundary conditions). We refer for instance to [Gri06] for the definition of
      the FK–Ising model (also called random cluster model of parameter q = 2) and for
      details about the coupling between Ising and FK–Ising. The following short proof
      is written as if the reader were familiar with this coupling.
          To prove the result, we rely on the fact that the box-crossing-property (i.e. the
      analogue of (BXP)) holds for critical FK–Ising percolation, see e.g. [DT19]. This
                                                  (δ)
      implies that, for the FK–Ising model on Λρn,n with wired boundary conditions, with
      non-negligible probability there exists a cluster that crosses Λρn,n but does not touch
                          (δ)
      the boundary of Λρn,n . If this cluster exists and that the sign +1 is assigned to it
      (which happens with conditional probability 1/2), then the crossing event holds for
      the Ising model. This implies the desired result.
      Proof in the case β < βc . By the general Russo–Seymour–Welsh theory developed
      in [KT23], the result holds if the probability measure is replaced by the (unique)
      infinite volume Gibbs measure at inverse temperature β. Indeed, this probability
      measure satisfies the FKG inequality, is invariant under the symmetries of the tri-
      angular lattice, and the probability of Crossn equals 1/2 under this measure; as a
      result, [KT23] implies the box-crossing property under this measure, see Theorem 1
      therein.12 By (SMP) and (MON), this implies the box-crossing property under
      µ+(δ) . The following exponentially fast spatial mixing result ends the proof.
        Λρn,n


      Exponentially fast spatial mixing. Assume that β < βc . Then, there exists
      C > 0 such that the following holds for every finite set V ⊂ T and every k ≥ 1. Let
      W be the set of vertices at (Euclidean) distance less than k from W . Then,
                                               −              −ck
                                 sup µ+
                                      W (A) − µW (A) ≤ C|V |e     ,
                                  A

      when the supremum is on every A ⊆ ΩW = {−1, +1}W that depends only on V .
      Proof. This result is (for instance) a consequence of (a) the coupling between the
      random cluster model of parameter q = 2 and the Ising model (see e.g. [Gri06])
      and (b) the sharpness of the phase transition of the random cluster model (see e.g.
      [DT19, Proposition 16]). We leave the details of the proof to the reader.
  12
     The only difference is that [KT23] considers measures on the edge configurations of Z2 that are
invariant under the symmetries of Z2 , but the proof in the case of site configurations on the triangular
lattice is exactly the same.


                                                   38
Remark A.2. The box-crossing property is most likely true with −1 boundary
conditions on Λρn,n , and even more generally for quads with ‘fractal’ boundary (see
[DMT21b] for such a result for random cluster models) but we have chosen to only
prove (BXP), for simplicity and because it is enough for our purpose.

crossing properties and spatial Markov properties imply that the exponent of this
event equals 2. In this paper, we only use that the exponent is at least two, which
is the following result, that we prove for completeness.

A.3.1       The infinitesimal generator
In this section, we prove the formula for the infinitesimal generator from Sec-

at x has rung exactly one time in the time interval [0, t] (i.e. #{Yx ∩([0, t]×[0, 1])} =
1), that no other clock has rung in this time interval, and that when the clock has
rung, the spin at x has changed. For every t > 0 and η ∈ Ωn , we have
